title: Productive meeting activities: leverage the team, empower the individual
summary: Jason Cohen lays out four meeting formats (ranting, ideation, decision-support, sparring practice), each defined by what one person needs from the room. He argues for declaring the type of conversation up front and keeping ownership with one individual, even when the boss is present.

principles.text: Meetings are best used to create something no one could make alone, while the decision stays with one person.
principles.quote: Meetings are most productive when we create something that none of us could have created alone.

principles.text: In ideation sessions, ask the group only to widen your options, not to pick one or decide your strategy.
principles.quote: I don't want you to solve the puzzle or decide which option is best, I just want you to help me see options that I'm not currently seeing.

principles.text: In decision-support, send your analysis ahead and ask for input. A vote is one input, not a verdict.
principles.quote: I might even ask the room to vote; not to dictate my future, but because I trust the room's opinion and I want it as another input in my decision process.

principles.text: Use sparring practice: invite Devil's Advocates to attack your work so it becomes bullet-proof, even from misinformed angles.
principles.quote: Whenever you see a brief, tight, bullet-proof document, it took a lot of work to get there.

principles.text: Declare the type of conversation you want so everyone participates correctly and facilitators can reroute it.
principles.quote: It's counterproductive when someone wants a Ranting, but receives a Sparring Practice. Declare what kind of conversation you want

principles.text: Name one owner for each decision. A decision owned by "us" is owned by no one; leaders should assist without usurping.
principles.quote: a decision made by "us" is owned by "no one," when in actual fact it *is* owned by X.
